Title: Is the game hurt by the open playing format?

Messages.Author: Eric Jome
Messages.Body:
This past weekend, I attended an Imperator storyline event. I did
very poorly of course; I've hardly played the game in the past 15
years and the other attendees were much more familiar with the game.

The day before the event, I re-read the rules again - my third read
through in 3 weeks. I really studied hard to play. I read a lot of
strategy articles. Built a deck that I guessed might not embarrass
itself too badly. And in general, the hours and hours of planning I
did worked out as well as I could expect... at least I didn't
humiliate myself too badly, I think.

Still, it was terribly obvious to me, essentially the new guy, that
this is going to be a nearly impossible game for me to get into for
one reason;

All cards for all time are all legal.

There's no way I can catch up on this in a pleasant way. I've already
spent dozens of hours studying hard to get the situation. The event I
played played into my existing (though very limited) knowledge of the
game and still that didn't help with almost every card every player
used resulting in a "what's that do?" from me...

So it was my impression that a completely open event, the NAC
qualifier I had considered going to next weekend, would be
impossible. How many different cards are there now? Several
thousand? I've played a lot (I mean A LOT) of CCGs, but I've never
seen one that the dominant play style was all cards all legal
forever... doesn't this just mean that the most degenerate strategies
stay dominant forever? That the learning curve for new players
becomes forever steeper until it is impossible to climb?

Eric Jome

Messages.Author: jcrossn...@gmail.com
Messages.Body:
Eric Jome wrote:
> So it was my impression that a completely open event, the NAC
> qualifier I had considered going to next weekend, would be
> impossible.  How many different cards are there now?  Several
> thousand?  I've played a lot (I mean A LOT) of CCGs, but I've never
> seen one that the dominant play style was all cards all legal
> forever... doesn't this just mean that the most degenerate strategies
> stay dominant forever?  That the learning curve for new players
> becomes forever steeper until it is impossible to climb?

It's true that the size of the available card pool is daunting for new
players, though one should become acquainted fairly quickly with most
of the cards you're likely to see at a tournament. The main things
that are important to know are the key cards from each discipline.
"What is likely to happen if I fight that guy?" and "How much is that
guy likely to bleed for if I tap out?" are very important questions to
learn the answers to. Also, VTES is multi-player and generally
somewhat informal, so it is always possible to ask someone at the
table what an opponent's deck is likely to do.

As for degenerate strategies, it isn't clear to me that VTES really
has any. There are some archetypes that are quite strong, but there is
quite a bit of diversity in the decks that show up to and win
tournaments.

Lately there have been a lot of people talking about set rotation for
some reason, but it seems to me that the vast majority of players
would prefer not to go down that route. The main reason for set
rotations, aside from forcing players to constantly update their
collections, seems to be that in most other CCGs one can win the game
more or less instantly by forming a single 2 or 3 card combo. As the
game gets older, more and more game ending combos come together from
the interactions of new and old cards, so you get set restriction to
make the game continue being a game. VTES just doesn't have those
combos, so set rotation is much less desirable.

Jesse

Eric, I understand your frustration. I also believe that if you made
yourself part of a playgroup that meets regularly, then you would be
"caught up" with 15 years of V:TES in about one month. The reason is
that when it comes to old cards, a group of them see play very often.
A larger group of older cards almost never see play. Once you play in
10 to 15 V:TES games, you will have seen most of the classic cards
that you will ever encounter.
It's a shame that the qualifier near you is so soon. If you had a
little bit more time, you could familiarize yourself with most of the
stuff we long time players would play at such an event.

Please hang in there.

Jay Kristoff, V:EKN Prince of Columbus, Ohio USA

Messages.Author: jcrossn...@gmail.com
Messages.Body:
>   It's a shame that the qualifier near you is so soon.  If you had a
> little bit more time, you could familiarize yourself with most of the
> stuff we long time players would play at such an event.

Also, it might not be your exact version of fun, but playing a simple
stealth bleed deck allows you to do very well without even necessarily
understanding what some other players are doing. Most of the standard
Kindred Spirits builds, for example, don't really care about much
other than what they're trying to do. If they get into combat, they
stand there and punch for 1, and hope they don't get killed too much.
They don't need to know much about voting beyond maybe having a few
titles to throw some weight around, and they most don't care about
cards on the table unless they grant intercept against your bleeds.

There are plenty of people out there (and many of them post frequently
on this and other online forums) who seem to think that stealth bleed
is uncool, and that everyone should be playing some trick combat combo
deck all the time. Those people are wrong. Stealth bleed is a great
way for new players to learn the game, and the fact that it works
doesn't make it cheesy. If you really want, you can sharpen your
skates for a trek up Everest after you've learned more of the game,
but if you stick to something simple and manageable you should do
quite well.

Jesse

Well, considering how little you've played over the years, you have nothing
to be ashamed of. And I think this speaks in favour of the game : not even a
good CCG player can master this one just by studying a few decklists and
strategy articles in such a short time !! It's a good, complex game, which
requires practice and hindsight.

> Still, it was terribly obvious to me, essentially the new guy, that
> this is going to be a nearly impossible game for me to get into for
> one reason;
>
> All cards for all time are all legal.
>

Yes, there is. With every big expansion come starter decks. They include
many important cards, and allow new players to get into the game very fast !
A few key cards are missing in the available starters as we speak, but that
still leaves dozens of very good decks feasible with, say, 2-3 starters and
a few boosters, so we're speaking less than 30-40 euros for a very
competitive deck here. Less if you already own some staple cards (as you
apparently do).

Not to mention that most of the playgroups have a "common box", where you'll
get all the cards we already have more than enough of. Oh, and it's a cheap
game compared to most, you can get some pretty good prices on cards on ebay
or at TheLasombra.com (excellent source for decklists too) and co.

> I've already
> spent dozens of hours studying hard to get the situation. The event I
> played played into my existing (though very limited) knowledge of the
> game and still that didn't help with almost every card every player
> used resulting in a "what's that do?" from me...

Yes, there are lots of cards, and it will take some time and practice. But
it will come sooner that you think. Fast enough, you'll be able to know the
key cards for the main disciplines, and the rest will follow. But there is
no shame in asking the card text for obscure cards, I do it often enough,
most of us do from time to time.

> So it was my impression that a completely open event, the NAC
> qualifier I had considered going to next weekend, would be
> impossible.

It's not impossible. It might be hard for you at that point. But if you play
a straight Dom / Obf bleed deck (or if you don't have any, switch to Dem
because there are some good starters available) you might even score some
nice points ! And it will certainly be a nice experience. Of course you'll
get better results next year with some practice, but it's a fun game to play
too, are results (and immediate ones) all you're after ?

> How many different cards are there now? Several
> thousand?

Sure. You can use a utility like FeldB http://member.rpg.hu/bala/feldb.html
or the Monger online, it will help you a lot !

> I've played a lot (I mean A LOT) of CCGs, but I've never
> seen one that the dominant play style was all cards all legal
> forever... doesn't this just mean that the most degenerate strategies
> stay dominant forever?

As has been said already, despite its vampires and other decaying undead,
Vampire isn't the degenerating type. ;-)

> That the learning curve for new players
> becomes forever steeper until it is impossible to climb?

Nope. Takes some time, but less than one might think, really.

We've got a group of players here in Paris who are very, very new to the
game, but they play a lot and have some previous game experience, and they
win many games already, so...

And as Jay said : it really doesn't matter if you never know what Call the
Lamprey, Twisting the Knife or Eyes of the Dead are. Some cards are
wallpaper, as in all CCG games, and you will never, ever see them
(especially not the ones that weren't reprinted).

Enjoy this game, it's one of the best around, and certainly the best
multi-player CCG ever !!

Orpheus

>doesn't this just mean that the most degenerate strategies
> stay dominant forever?  

Degenerate is a emotionally charged word. A strong deck back in 1994
can still be a strong deck now, but you don't need cards from 1994 to
build a strong deck now. In fact a saw a weenie princes deck using
all Jyhad cards (era 1994) make it to the finals of the Dallas
Qualifier (1 person out of 5). It didn't win, but it shows that older
cards are neither obsolete nor overpowered.

>That the learning curve for new players
> becomes forever steeper until it is impossible to climb?

There certainly is a steep learning curve for VTES, but it is the best
game I have ever played. It is best to play enough to familiarize
yourself with the game (as is true for all games).

All in all, this is a game that allows players to enter and exit the
game and then re-enter the game without having to make another large
financial commitment.

Eric, I totally get what you mean, and please don't take this the
wrong way, but:
Why did you sign up for a storyline if you've been out of the game so
long? That's a type of competitive play format. Of course people who
attend those games know (almost) all the cards and tricks and stuff.
No offense, seriously, but you don't sign up for Wimbledon if you're
not yet familiar with all the ins and outs of tennis, either.

I totally understand how your experience sucked, and that is a great
shame because VTES is so much fun. But I think you're totally rushing
things and blaming it on the card pool.

What you should do, is just play a bunch of friendly games. Get to
know the game, and all those cards, by seeing them in action. But
without much actually depending on you doing well or not (no
embarrasments at all).
Find some folks who are willing to give you a bit of leeway when
playing, i.e. let you get away with bad plays sometimes, and who are
willing to teach you stuff. Ask them to play as many different decks
as possible so you can learn what is out there.

In other words: don't study the rules and then dive straight into a
competition, just play. Then, after a while, you'll know all the
current 'standard card functions' and you'll see that most cards can
be seen as variations on each other (this is true for every CCG, is it
not?). Meaning that in the future, a card you don't know can quickly
be explained as "just like <a card X you know>, but with <difference
from card X>".

You'll also find that the non-set rotation is a good thing.
I understand that you were playing 15 years ago. Your cards from that
era are still legal AND good to play with (except of course for the
ones that already sucked back then). Now that's value for money, no?

Just give yourself time to get adjusted to the stuff that came out in
the meantime. The 'main game' really hasn't changed, so I'm sure
you'll pick it all up in no time.

Eric, I know that Chicago is a little far for you to travel to play,
especially on a weeknight, but please keep an eye on VTES_Chicago on
google groups. Friday night, I attempted to have a game night at my
house, which is in Volo, about an hour from Milwaukee. Since I drive
home at least an hour and a half from Chicago when we play on Thursday
nights, that shouldn't be too much of a hardship... Anyway, we had to
call it off due to lack of interest, but if you were free on Friday,
then we probably could have played.

I do agree that learning as you go in a tournament isn't ideal, and I
think you would have just as hard a time with any other game. After
playing a handful of casual games, I think you'll end up with a much
better understanding of the card pool. And it's not really unfair to
ask people to declare what their cards do when they play them. Even
after playing for ~15 years, I still occasionally have to ask for
clarification on cards that have been around since Dark Sovereigns
(usually more of a fine point than "what the hell does that do?", but
certain cards from other sets are still played rarely enough that just
hearing the name doesn't immediately remind me of what it does).

I don't understand set rotation, and never did. Sure, it helps newer
players keep up, but it leaves experienced players with a lot of
worthless cardboard. I quit playing L5R shortly after they went to a
Type 2-style tournament format. Luckily when I played M:TG, type 2
was only barely heard of and type 1 was the dominant tournament format
- I quit for other reasons. I probably would've liked type 2 for a
little bit, since I wouldn't have had to deal with Moxes and such,
although type 1.5 took care of that; but half the fun of a new set is
seeing what kind of combos it brings up for older cards and what old
strategies it might revitalize. I would hate to have things dumbed
down to where you just have a pool of cards from the last 3 sets to
make a deck out of...

I mentioned set rotation in another thread so I guess I'm qualified to
answer this.

> The main reason for set
> rotations, aside from forcing players to constantly update their
> collections, seems to be that in most other CCGs one can win the game
> more or less instantly by forming a single 2 or 3 card combo. As the
> game gets older, more and more game ending combos come together from
> the interactions of new and old cards, so you get set restriction to
> make the game continue being a game. VTES just doesn't have those
> combos, so set rotation is much less desirable.

I suspect that it's the other way around. You get game ending combos
because new cards are intentionally designed, playtested and balanced
in the context of the currently legal block. VTES doesn't have them
because new cards are created with every other set in mind.

The former approach to designing is obviously bad for the players. If
unrestricted tournament formats are neglected a player can either play
a bad and unbalanced game or keep up with the newest sets. I don't
think anybody would want VTES to go that way. However, having an
occasional set restricted tournament couldn't do any damage as long as
the game continues to be designed with the unrestricted format in mind.

Messages.Author: vladc...@gmail.com
Messages.Body:
Even if this thread has already been dismissed, just a couple
thoughts.As mentioned, the game reprints frequently, so access to key
cards is easy. One could argue this is stagnant which may be true
since you still have prevalence of certain cards like Govern or decks
like Malk 94 still running around, but at the same time, new cards
that come out, in a way similar to other games, change the archetypes
somewhat or develop new ones. Cool because the decks you love are
relevant, not cool because not enough new stuff really shakes things
up. Also cards do enough similar things that if you don’t have access
to card A, card B will do in a pinch.

The game is also well suited for open since as mentioned, the game
doesn’t rely on cheap combos that break the game in five minutes and
it’s simply a race to see which player pulls the best broken cards
first out of their nearly identical decks. So there’s no real need to
get ‘problem’ cards out of the environment or reset the game because
of a horde of design mistakes. Conversely there is no need to
continually increase the power level of cards and make older ones
obsolete because the game plays well and doesn’t need cards like
“bleed at +5 bleed, and +5 stealth” or “burn your prey’s tapped
minions at +3 stealth” to maintain interest. After that gets old, what
next? A reset to make games longer, so rotate those out, and go back
to bleeding at +1 and +1?

To sum up, set rotation is unnecessary and even detrimental in a game
like VTES because:

a) Reprints are accessible and frequent.
b) No real problem combos or decks exist necessitating rotation to
rescale game.
c) Power climb would be bad because game is fairly balanced as is.
Instead, tech should be created to resolve outstanding issues, or
create new and balanced themes.
d) Enough variation and repeating abilities on similar cards allows
use of one card if a similar card is not available for whatever
reason.
e) Mechanics in game are the same as they were initially so even
though there are a lot of different cards, they all do variations on a

On Jun 8, 12:54 pm, Jay Kristoff <jaykrist...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Eric,  I understand your frustration.  I also believe that if you made
> yourself part of a playgroup that meets regularly, then you would be
> "caught up" with 15 years of V:TES in about one month.  The reason is
> that when it comes to old cards, a group of them see play very often.
> A larger group of older cards almost never see play.  Once you play in
> 10 to 15 V:TES games, you will have seen most of the classic cards
> that you will ever encounter.

> Please hang in there.

I'll echo Jay's comments. If you play with four other people and
get two or three games in a play session, you'll see eight or twelve
decks' worth of cards in a few hours. Precisely because of the
3000+ card environment, no one will give you any trouble if you
ask to read a card, or ask what a card does, or how it interacts
with another card. I have to do this all the time, even though I've
been playing for over ten years. Don't sweat it.

Regarding whether the 3000+ card environment is a bar to new
players: I believe it is not. Since you describe your background
as having played numerous card games, you may be familiar with
games where Strategy X or Deck Z is dominant, and on the
tournament scene everyone plays that deck or a deck designed
to thwart it. This is not the case with V:TES, in my opinion,
because of the 3000+ card environment. You can build a deck
that does well in an area of the game - bleeding, voting, combat,
etc. - and you can do quite well. You can bring that same deck
to another table and do poorly. Your opponents, their decks and
their play styles will do more to determine table outcomes than
playing teh n3w c00lness from tha intarwebs.

In a given block of Magic: the Gathering, you might have four
or five strong strategies for tournament play, and one of those
will best fit your own play style and the local metagame. In
V:TES you have 15 years of strong strategies - you will not be
able to successfully account for all of them. This makes your
gamesmanship and ability to play your own deck in a fluid
environment more important. Pick a weapon and get into the
arena.

Here's a story from my own experience: after a few months'
worth of poor showing, I decided to play a horrid, awful, cheesy,
Dominate weenie deck at a qualifier. I just wanted a win, that's
all. And boy, did I get some. I swept a few tables in the qualifying
rounds and was a lock for the finals -- and this was in very strong,
capable competition. I went to the finals confident and feeling
good. In the finals, my prey got out a single vampire with Atonement:
+1 intercept (all that was needed to stop my Govern the Unaligned)
and this vampire does not tap when blocking younger vampires
(all of my vampires were younger). And voila, my game was over.
I stayed in there, tried to haggle and offer help to other players
in return for VPs or assistance, but it was to no avail. And that
will
just happen sometimes, even with a strong deck.

V:TES is not impossible to get into. It may require a different
mindset to try and get a handle on the metagame. But if you
think you might be interested in the politics of multi-player tables
and you think you have a knack for a given type of play, you
should definitely give it a try. Generally speaking, VTES players
love to see new blood. (Har. It is a pun.)

--plus, changing to a retirement/rotational system now would
basically bankrupt the game's long-running principle against
such marketing models. Which would be a shame.

hza

On Jun 8, 3:13 pm, Eric Jome <eric.j...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Well, this rather quickly became a discussion about me and my play
> experience, but I had been hoping to talk more about what it means for
> the game to have no set restrictions ever.

I think a lot of people already addressed this, but I'll certainly
throw in. Yeah, having no set restrictions at all means that there is
a *lot* of stuff floating around to keep track of (What is Black Hand?
What are Imbued? What is a Laibon? Anarchs?). But for the most part,
the issues aren't really the small specifics, but the large strategy
issues, and they are pretty consistent across the game--yeah, the
Malkavians and the Lasombra and the Giovanni and the Kisayid all can
Stealth and Bleed (for example), and they all do it a little
differently. But it is all Stealth and Bleed, and interacts the same
way Stealth and Bleed interacts, pretty much regardless of which kind
it is.

The advantage of no set rotation is the obvious--all cards are always
good. Which means people who played for a few years in 1995, left the
game, and came back now can still sit down and play a competitive game
with what they already own. Yeah, again, new folks coming in now have
a lot to keep up with, but really, again, the game is mostly about
large strategy issues (Stealth and Bleed vs Rush vs Vote Decks vs Wall
vs Weenie Horde) much more than the little specifics (What does that
Osebo do?). After a few games, most of the standard cards become old
hat, and yeah, every once and a while, something will surprise you
(I've been playing this game regularly and consistently for 12+ years
now, and *I* still say "Huh. That card does *that*? Crazy!" every few
games)., but the basic strategies are what you need to figure out.
Yeah, a crazy Assamite Anarch stealth vote deck is good and uses all
sorts of crazy tech, but it is still just a stealth vote deck.

-Peter

> So, in the end, I guess I've learned the answer to my question;

V:TES is hardly the only CCG to have survived for a while and allowed
cards from any sets. All such games seem offputting to new players to
me. Mechanics bloat is a huge problem with CCGs. There's at least
two CCGs that I demoed for years that I lost interest in trying to
teach because there were just too many parts.

With V:TES, which has a steep learning curve to begin with, mechanics
bloat can make it nigh impenetrable, sure.

On the other hand, I find that some things overwhelm people unfamiliar
with lots of cards that shouldn't. The number of different effects in
the game that matter isn't nearly as large as the number of different
effects. One thing that creates a vampire is much like another, as
stealth cards are like each other, intercept cards like each other,
bleed cards like each other, etc.

But, then, while you will tend to see many of the same cards played
across games, V:TES has a much, much higher percentage of playable
cards than the typical two-player CCG and, of course, has lots of
sets.

It might actually be easier to become a competitive player of this
game than a casual player. The casual player is going to focus on
cards - which cards are cool, which clans are cool. The competitive
player can step back from worrying about thousands of different card
texts and be concerned with the strategic game. Is it more important
to understand the difference between Ecstatic Agony and Lessons in the
Steel or to understand the difference between how to play 4 player
tables vs. 5?

I've certainly come across much better players than I who knew far
less about card texts.

I regularly game in groups of 8 to 20. Most of the board games
popular today take a minimum of 4 players. Even in a gaming
environment that has mostly 2 player games, there are often many
people gathered to play many matches of 2 player games. To me, people
seem like the least problem...

But having people develop an interest seems to be a problem. The game
is very complex. People shy away from long, complex games to play
easier, faster games. To relate a similar story, friends and I have
had no trouble agreeing communally to each buy a handful of Magic
cards and play that in a limited league format. Yet, when we talk
about growing the league into more open play, interest breaks down...
and that's only "more open" in the sense that we would move to playing
with more than 200 cards each, still in the current sets in
production.

If I take these same people and tell them, oh by the way, if you like
Anarchs you'll be shopping eBay praying for an OOP set to come up at
10 times the price, that's a deal breaker. If I take these same
people and say "yeah, that Malkavian stealth bleed deck you hated in
1995 is still an active thriving part of the game", that's a deal
breaker too.

Eric Jome

The first part isn't really all that true. The original Anarch set was
mostly terrible, and the newer stuff from Twilight Rebellion is much
much better. Also, a bunch of the better anarch cards were recently
reprinted as promos for the last storyline, so they are definitely in
circulation still. It is annoying that the Fee Stakes haven't been
reprinted. I'll definitely give you that one.

The second part could totally go either way though. Instead of "the
Malkavian deck you hated in 1995 is still legal" you could say "the
Toreador deck you loved in 1995 is still legal", or whatever. Also,
despite the fact that people habitually refer to Malk94 as a cheesy
high powered deck, it's actually fairly rare at all levels of play, at
least in my experience, and I honestly don't think it's very good
anymore.

Ah -

That's the issue in a nutshell. Knowing nothing about designing
software or web design, I don't really notice the clunky interface, I
just want to play. As an expert, you can't help but notice it, and it
prevents you from playing.

It's like for me, going into crappy game stores can be a very painful
experience, having owned one for many many years. I can't help but
notice the poorly trained staff, the disgusting shelves, the lack of new
product etc etc. Even though the store may have had what I wanted, I
might not stay long enough to shop for it.

That said, the JOL interface is very cross platform friendly, and one
big thing about it - you don't have to commit to a block of time to
play. You can just check your games, update your situation if
necessary, and come back later. You *can* play in real-time as well,
but you don't have to. That grants it flexibility over other VtES
playing platforms, like Lackey.

And finally, it's too bad you don't want to try JOL again - it really is
a great place to practice VTES. And even though it might seem tough to
get started, once you do, it becomes a snap.

best -

chris
